passage:
Paulo checked the calendar on his phone for the third time. There it was: Thursday, 6 p.m., café shift, and underneath, Told Jin Monday. He had even written that.
Still, when he got home, Jin was sitting in the dark. "You never said you were working. You just disappear and expect me to guess."
"I told you on Monday, remember? At the laundromat."
"That didn't happen. You always do this. You rewrite things so you look good."
Paulo opened his mouth, then closed it. Last week it had been the concert tickets, and before that the rent money. Each time Jin was certain, and each time Paulo ended up saying sorry.
"Sorry," he said now. "Maybe I forgot to say."
Later, washing dishes in their Melbourne flat, he noticed he had started writing everything down, and still didn't trust it. He wasn't sure anymore whether he was a forgetful person, or had only been told he was.

qa.q: What had Paulo written under the Thursday shift in his calendar?
qa.a: He had written "Told Jin Monday" under the café shift.

qa.q: What is Paulo feeling as he washes the dishes?
qa.a: He feels confused and less sure of himself, no longer knowing whether he is truly forgetful or has only been told he is.

qa.q: What could Paulo do the next time his note and Jin's version clash?
qa.a: He could trust his written note, calmly say he remembers it differently without apologising, and check his experience with someone he trusts outside the flat.

qa.q: What would change if Jin said "I don't remember that, maybe I missed it" instead?
qa.a: The disagreement would be about a missed message, not about Paulo's mind, and he would not need to apologise for something that was not wrong.

grounding: A young man repeatedly told he rewrites events starts apologising for things he did not do and doubts even his own written notes.

passage:
"Ishita, you uploaded the wrong data file again," Tarun said loudly across the chemistry lab, so the whole bench heard.
Ishita's cheeks burned. She was almost sure she had uploaded the file he sent her at midnight. Almost. All semester Tarun had told her she misheard the meeting time, that she overreacted when he took credit for her graphs, that she "always gets emotional". Somewhere along the way, almost sure had become the most she ever felt.
"Sorry, sorry, my fault," she said, before checking anything.
Professor Rao looked up from the fume hood. "Let's see the shared folder." The file history showed Tarun had sent that file at 12:04 a.m.
Tarun shrugged. "Whatever, small thing."
Ishita stared at the screen. She had apologised for his mistake, again, without a second's thought. On the walk back to the hostel she counted how many times she had said sorry that week, and stopped at eleven.

qa.q: What did the file history show?
qa.a: The file history showed Tarun had sent that file at 12:04 a.m.

qa.q: What does Ishita's instant "Sorry, sorry, my fault" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels anxious and ashamed, no longer trusting her own memory, and rushes to take the blame even when almost sure she isn't at fault.

qa.q: What small step could Ishita take the next time Tarun blames her?
qa.a: She could pause and check the record before apologising, keep her own notes of shared work, and talk it over with Professor Rao or someone she trusts.

qa.q: How might Professor Rao see what happened at the bench?
qa.a: Professor Rao seems to want facts rather than accusations and, after seeing the file history, may realise Ishita has been taking blame that was not hers.

grounding: A student told all semester that she mishears and overreacts apologises by reflex for Tarun's mistake and notices how far her confidence has shrunk.

passage:
I'm Asif, and in my second year I shared a flat with Pradeep. I only understood what was happening months later.
It started small. "You never told me your parents were visiting." I was sure I had. "You're misremembering." Then: "I didn't say I'd pay the electricity bill. You always twist things." Then: "You're overreacting again."
After a while, I stopped trusting myself. I said sorry for things I didn't do. I wrote everything in a notebook so I could check later. I became quieter in class, too, unsure of even small facts.
One day, looking for something else, I scrolled back through our old chat. There it was: "My parents are coming on the 12th." And his reply: "cool." There were five more like that.
I sat on my bed and felt dizzy. It wasn't my memory. It was the constant telling.
I showed the chat to my friend Ravi that evening, and started looking for a new flat.

qa.q: What did Asif find in the old chat?
qa.a: "My parents are coming on the 12th," and Pradeep's reply, "cool."

qa.q: How did Asif feel when he found the old chat?
qa.a: Asif felt dizzy and shaken, realising his memory had been right all along and the constant telling had shrunk his confidence.

qa.q: What steps did Asif take after finding proof?
qa.a: Asif showed the chat to a friend, Ravi, that evening and started looking for a new flat.

qa.q: Why might Pradeep keep saying Asif misremembers?
qa.a: Pradeep may want to avoid blame for things like the electricity bill, and constant correcting shifts responsibility onto Asif.

grounding: A young adult recalls being told repeatedly of misremembering, apologising for things that weren't wrong, and finding proof the memory was right.

passage:
College counsellor's note, Monday.
Urmila, second-year commerce, came in today. In the first ten minutes she apologised six times: for being late, for talking too much, for "probably making this up."
She has been with Hrithik for a year. She described how often he tells her she remembers things wrong, that she's too emotional, that "a normal girlfriend wouldn't get upset about this." She now checks her own messages before saying anything, in case she's wrong again.
She said, "I used to be good at remembering things. Now I don't trust my own head." Her hands were twisting a tissue into shreds.
I told her that feeling muddled and less sure of yourself are real effects of being told over and over that you're wrong, and that it is not her fault.
We agreed she will keep a simple written record, and meet me again on Thursday. I gave her the number of the women's helpline in case she ever feels unsafe.

qa.q: How many times did Urmila apologise in the first ten minutes?
qa.a: She apologised six times.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling as she twisted the tissue?
qa.a: Urmila felt anxious and confused, no longer trusting her own mind after being told so often that she was wrong.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take?
qa.a: The counsellor told her it was not her fault, agreed on a written record and a Thursday meeting, and gave her the women's helpline number.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see his comments?
qa.a: Hrithik may see them as just correcting her, not realising or not admitting that they have shrunk her confidence.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young adult repeatedly told she misremembers, now apologising constantly and distrusting her own mind.

passage:
Thursday night
Rashmi said it again today. "You never told me you had an exam, Sangeeta. You're making it up." I KNOW I told her. I told her on Sunday while she was making tea. I think.
This is the fourth time this month. Last week she said I "always exaggerate" when I said the room was cold. The week before, that I "imagined" her reading my diary.
Now I've started apologising first, just in case. Sorry if I didn't tell you. Sorry if I'm remembering wrong. Sorry, sorry.
I bought a small notebook and started writing things down with the date. Today I checked it: "Sunday, told Rashmi about maths exam Thursday." It's right there. In my handwriting.
I cried a bit when I saw it. Relief, and something else. How long have I been doubting myself?
Tomorrow I'm going to call my sister and tell her all of it.
Sangeeta

qa.q: What did Sangeeta write in her notebook on Sunday?
qa.a: "Sunday, told Rashmi about maths exam Thursday."

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when she checked her notebook?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt relieved and upset at once, crying because she realised how long she'd been doubting herself.

qa.q: What is Sangeeta planning to do next?
qa.a: Sangeeta plans to call Sangeeta's sister tomorrow and tell her everything, reaching someone outside the situation.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see her own comments?
qa.a: Rashmi may think she is just correcting Sangeeta, perhaps to avoid being wrong herself.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult repeatedly told of misremembering or exaggerating, apologising in advance and losing trust in memory.
